subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: learning a rule from the mistake [Revision]
passage: By noon Abena remembered: the bird feeder in the yard in Accra was empty, and she had promised her mother to fill it before school on Friday. Two sparrows sat on the fence, waiting. Her stomach dropped. She went to her mother in the kitchen. "Mama, I forgot the birds yesterday. It is my fault." Mama nodded slowly. "Thank you for telling me. They were hungry, but they are fine." Abena filled the feeder at once. Then she asked, "Can I set a reminder on your phone for every morning?" Mama handed it over. Abena typed BIRDS for seven o'clock, then carried the seed box from the shed to the shelf by the window, where she would see it while brushing her teeth.

qa.q: Where did Abena put the seed box?
qa.a: She put the seed box on the shelf by the window.

qa.q: How did Abena feel when she saw the empty feeder?
qa.a: Guilty and worried, since her stomach dropped when she noticed the two waiting sparrows.

qa.q: What else could Abena do besides the reminder?
qa.a: Put a tick chart beside the feeder, because seeing it each morning keeps the promise in mind.

qa.q: How might Mama see Abena's confession?
qa.a: With appreciation, since she thanked Abena for telling her and let Abena set the reminder on her phone.

grounding: A girl who forgot to feed the birds is honest about it, then sets a phone reminder and moves the seed box where she will see it.

passage: I am Tushar and my desk is behind Radhika's, so I heard it. Before maths, Ramesh leaned over and whispered, "Show me your answers, just this once?" Radhika kept her page flat. "No, Ramesh. But I will go through the steps with you after class if you like." Ramesh rolled his eyes and turned away. I thought that was the end of their friendship. But at the bell Radhika waited beside his desk with her notebook, and they went to the corridor bench, where she drew out the steps of long division. Ramesh was frowning, but he was writing. I cannot know if he was still annoyed. When the next bell rang he said, "Okay, one more."

qa.q: What did Radhika offer to do instead of showing her answers?
qa.a: She offered to go through the steps with Ramesh after class.

qa.q: What might Ramesh have felt when Radhika said no?
qa.a: Annoyed and embarrassed, since he rolled his eyes and turned away, though Tushar cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Radhika do if Ramesh keeps asking for answers?
qa.a: Repeat the offer to study together, because she can hold firm without ending the friendship.

qa.q: How might Radhika see Ramesh's request to copy?
qa.a: Radhika will not show her answers, but she still wants to help, so she offers to go through the steps with him after class.

grounding: A friend asks to copy the maths answers, and the girl says no while offering to explain the method after class.

subtype: Approach: thinking of what the test is for [Thinking]
passage: Vishal's friend Zainab tapped his shoulder before the fractions test and mouthed, "Answers?" Vishal's pencil hovered. It would be easy. Two minutes, and she would get her marks. But then what? If she copies, the teacher thinks she knows fractions. Next chapter is ratios, and fractions sit inside ratios. She will be lost, and I will have helped her get lost. Marks would come today; learning would not. He turned his paper a little, shook his head and whispered, "I will help you learn it after school. Copying will not help you." Zainab sighed but nodded. Vishal felt his hands go steady.

qa.q: Which chapter did Vishal think would come after fractions?
qa.a: Vishal thought the next chapter would be ratios.

qa.q: How was Vishal feeling while his pencil hovered, and what made him decide?
qa.a: Whether giving Zainab the answers truly helps her, and he realised it would give marks without learning, so he felt torn but chose to refuse. 😅

qa.q: What other approach could Vishal use to help Zainab?
qa.a: Offer to study together after school, because then she learns the method she needs for the next chapter.

qa.q: How might Zainab see Vishal's refusal?
qa.a: Disappointed at first, since she sighed, but she nodded, so she may come to see that he wants her to understand.

grounding: A boy reasons that copying gives marks but no learning, so helping a friend cheat does not truly help.

subtype: Approach: giving in to keep the friendship [Pitfall]
passage: Under the neem tree the class-five bench was white with chalk dust. During the Hindi test Ganga whispered, "Sahil, show me number three." Sahil shook his head, and Ganga turned her face away. "Fine. I will not talk to you at lunch." That was the sentence he feared. So he tilted his slate. Ganga copied quickly. All afternoon Sahil's stomach felt tight. What if Sir noticed two identical answers? Both would be blamed. Would Ganga even stay friends after this? The worry grew every time he looked at the door of the headmaster's room. By the walk home it had swallowed the pleasure of having a friend back.

qa.q: What did Ganga say she would do if Sahil refused?
qa.a: Ganga said she would not talk to him at lunch.

qa.q: What was Sahil afraid of when he tilted his slate?
qa.a: That Ganga would stop talking to him and stop being his friend, and afterwards he also feared that both would be blamed.

qa.q: What could Sahil have done instead?
qa.a: Say no kindly and offer to study together, because the friendship can survive a refusal and neither child gets in trouble.

qa.q: How might the teacher see two identical answers?
qa.a: As a sign that one child copied, and the teacher may blame both because it is hard to tell who wrote it first.

grounding: A boy shows his answers because he fears losing his friend, then worries that the teacher will blame them both.

passage: I am Samir and I was packing my bag when I heard Tejas say to his friend Meghna, "Show me the science answers tomorrow, please. I will fail otherwise." Meghna shook her head. But instead of walking off, she said, "How about this: come to my place on Sunday at four. We go through the chapter together, and you write your own answers." Tejas looked surprised. "You would do that?" "Bring your notebook and a snack." Tejas nodded slowly, biting his lip. I do not know if he wanted to study or only wanted the answers, but he wrote SUNDAY 4 on his palm.

qa.q: What did Tejas write on his palm?
qa.a: He wrote SUNDAY 4 on his palm.

qa.q: What was Tejas worried about when he asked for the answers?
qa.a: Failing, since he said he would fail otherwise.

qa.q: What else could Meghna add if Tejas still wants only answers?
qa.a: Explain why copying will not help him in the exam itself and suggest asking the teacher for extra help, because the real problem is fear of failing.

qa.q: How might Meghna's offer have felt to Tejas?
qa.a: Surprising and a relief, since he asked "You would do that?" and nodded slowly. 🙂

grounding: A girl suggests studying together on Sunday so her friend can prepare properly instead of copying.

subtype: Approach: telling the teacher when the friend will not stop [Revision]
passage: I am Shreya, and on Monday I saw Kabir on the stairs looking as if he had swallowed a stone. He had said no to his friend Salma twice about copying in the annual exam, and then he heard that Salma planned to bring a chit inside a pencil box. At break he walked to the staffroom door and asked his teacher Ms Iyer if he could talk to her alone. He was in there for five minutes. When he came out his face was red, and he said only, "I am not sure that was right, but it would have been worse." I do not know how he feels about Salma now, and I did not ask.

qa.q: Where did Salma plan to hide the chit?
qa.a: Salma planned to bring it inside a pencil box.

qa.q: How did Kabir seem to feel after speaking to Ms Iyer?
qa.a: Uneasy but resolved, since his face was red and he said he was not sure it was right but that it would have been worse.

qa.q: What other step could Kabir add for his friendship with Salma?
qa.a: He could tell Salma honestly why he spoke up and offer to help Salma study, because it shows he acted out of concern.

qa.q: How might Ms Iyer see Kabir coming to her?
qa.a: As a serious step, since he asked to talk alone and stayed five minutes, and she can now deal with a problem before the exam.

grounding: After refusing twice, a boy learns the friend plans a chit and tells the teacher privately, judging it worth stopping the bigger problem.

subtype: Approach: thinking that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage: Monday. In the canteen Ira said, "Half the class copies in tests. It is normal." She kept her diary tilted for peeking later and thought nothing of it. Wednesday. During the science test she copied one answer from the next bench, glancing up between words. Omkar Sir was suddenly beside her desk. He took her paper without a word. Thursday. In the corridor Ira learned that the test would count as zero and a note had gone home to her parents. "But everyone does it," she told a friend. "Did everyone get a zero?" her friend asked. Ira did not answer. Her cheeks burned.

qa.q: What happened to Ira's science test?
qa.a: It counted as zero, and a note went home to her parents.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when her friend asked whether everyone got a zero?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stung, since she did not answer and her cheeks burned.

qa.q: What could Ira do instead of copying, and why?
qa.a: Ask the teacher for help or study with a friend beforehand, because that builds real answers without risking a zero.

qa.q: How might Omkar Sir see Ira's habit?
qa.a: As breaking a rule however common it is, since he took her paper without a word.

grounding: A girl tells herself everyone copies, but when caught in a test finds it is still against the rule and has consequences.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing a light reply to avoid a fight [Thinking]
passage: Only five minutes of lunch were left, the corridor was loud, and Akash, a friend of Mridul's, was already walking towards Mridul with his maths notebook open. Mridul knew what was coming. He had rehearsed on the stairs: not "That is cheating", which would sound like a lecture, but something about himself. "Akash, I do not want trouble with Ma'am. Sorry, I cannot." He had said it in his head twice. When Akash reached him and asked for the homework answers, Mridul swallowed, then said it aloud. Akash shrugged, a little stiff. "Okay, fine." No sulking. Mridul's shoulders dropped. It had been easier than he feared, mostly because he had made it about himself.

qa.q: What reason did Mridul plan to give?
qa.a: He planned to say he did not want trouble with Ma'am.

qa.q: Why did Mridul choose that reason instead of calling it cheating?
qa.a: He worried a lecture would upset Akash and wanted to refuse without judging his friend.

qa.q: What could Mridul offer along with the refusal?
qa.a: Offer to explain the method after class, because it helps Akash without breaking the rules.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt at the refusal?
qa.a: Slightly stiff or disappointed but not insulted, since he shrugged and said okay without sulking.

grounding: A boy prepares a refusal that sounds about himself, not a judgement on his friend, so it is easier to accept.

subtype: Approach: tempted by fear of failing [Thinking]
passage: My name is Harish, and I remember the fractions test because my eyes kept sliding to the left. Bhavesh's page was right there, full of numbers. My pencil shook. I did not want another low mark, because last time Papa had gone quiet at dinner. Then something odd happened: I looked at the fear instead of the page. It was the fear that wanted me to peek, not me. I put my eyes back on my own paper and did what I could. Next morning I stayed after class and told Nirmala Ma'am, "I get scared in tests. Can you help me with fractions?" She smiled and gave me two evenings a week.

qa.q: What did Harish ask Nirmala Ma'am for?
qa.a: Harish asked for help with fractions.

qa.q: What did Harish realise about the urge to peek?
qa.a: That fear of another low mark was what made it tempting.

qa.q: What else could Harish do to ease test fear?
qa.a: Practise a few timed questions at home, because familiarity lowers the worry.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Ma'am see Harish's request?
qa.a: As an honest and brave step, since she smiled and offered two evenings a week.

grounding: A child afraid of low marks feels the pull to peek at a nearby page, names the fear, and asks the teacher for help instead.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent what to do about a friend [Action]
passage: Thursday night. Told Amma about Varun. Today at the quiz I saw him look at a chit in his geometry box. I do not know what to do. If I tell Ma'am, is that telling on a friend? If I do not, I am keeping a secret that feels heavy. Amma listened to everything, then said, "Being kind and being honest can go together. Start with Varun. Tell him what you saw and that you are worried for him. If he does not stop, a teacher needs to know, and you can say it is because you care." I feel less tangled. Tomorrow I will talk to Varun at recess. My heart is already thumping. Ishita

qa.q: Where did Ishita see Varun's chit?
qa.a: Ishita saw the chit in Varun's geometry box.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when deciding what to do?
qa.a: Torn and worried, since telling might feel like telling on a friend but keeping quiet felt heavy. 😰

qa.q: What should Ishita do if Varun keeps cheating after the talk?
qa.a: Tell a teacher and explain that it comes from care, as Amma suggested.

qa.q: How might Varun feel when Ishita tells him what was seen?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed or defensive at first, but he may also feel that someone cares, since the concern is for him.

grounding: Ishita, unsure whether telling on a friend is right, talks it over with Amma, who shows how to be kind and honest at once.
